records.name: Para
records.summary:
Pará recorded 5 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, in the middle band of the association dossier's ranking of that year's 80 national killings. No Pará-specific statute, ordinance or policy affecting trans people was found in the audited sources, so there is no documented local legal hostility or local protection to weigh; the national framework applies uniformly.

For a trans visitor the operative risk is geographic: roughly two-thirds to 68% of such killings nationally occur in interior cities outside the capitals, where monitoring, denunciation and access to public policy are weaker, and victims are overwhelmingly young Black travestis and trans women killed in public places. A visitor travelling beyond the main metropolitan area lands precisely where the recorded killings sit — the least-monitored geography.

sources.summary: SBT News (26 Jan 2026) reports ANTRA's 9th annual dossier: 80 trans and travesti people killed in Brazil in 2025, a ~34% fall year-on-year, Brazil first in world rankings; victims overwhelmingly travestis and trans women, killed with extreme violence. National dossier — the table behind this record's 2025 state count. Supplies this record's 2025 count (5 of 80).

Sergipe Em Debate (27 Jan 2025): ANTRA's previous-year dossier recorded 122 trans and travesti killings in Brazil in 2024, 16% below 2023, five of the victims rights defenders. Companion dossier this record cites for its 2024 comparison year. This record uses it to note Pará's 2024 position cannot be fixed from the audited sources.

records.name: Alagoas
records.summary:
Alagoas recorded 6 killings of trans and travesti people in 2024 — among the elevated small-state totals in that year's dossier table — and just 2 in 2025. No Alagoas-specific legal restriction or enforcement finding is documented; the national framework applies uniformly.

The swing between consecutive dossiers on a small population is itself the visitor-relevant finding: at these denominators a couple of cases moves the state's position sharply, and the monitoring body cautions that falling national counts partly reflect violence shifting into attempted homicides rather than improving safety. Places the risk wherever a visibly trans person is in public: the dossiers' regional victim profile — young, Black, poor, killed in public places at night — makes open visibility the operative hazard, and the state sits inside the country's hardest-hit region.

National dossier — the table behind this record's 2025 state count. Supplies this record's 2025 count (2 of 80).

CNN Brasil (27 Jan 2025) on ANTRA's 2024 dossier: Brazil led world trans-killings rankings for a 16th consecutive year with 122 killed in 2024 (16% below 2023); victims mostly young, Black women, many from the Northeast; crimes marked by extreme violence. Source behind this record's 2024 count and its year-over-year comparison. Supplies this record's 2024 count (6).

records.name: Distrito Federal
records.summary:
The Distrito Federal recorded 2 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, a low absolute count for a major metropolitan area. Brasília is the seat of the STF, the national protective apparatus, and the offices of human-rights bodies; ANTRA's own Dossiê is compiled and reported from DF desks. The capital hosts international diplomatic missions and NGO infrastructure that raise the visibility and institutional cost of anti-trans violence.

These factors justify a modest positive deviation of about 0.02 above the national 0.71. Compared with São Paulo (0.71, no deviation), which also leads in institutional capacity but recorded 4 killings in 2025 and 16 in 2024, the DF's lower absolute numbers and concentration of protective infrastructure make it marginally safer for a visitor. The 2 killings against ~3 million population give a rate of ~0.67/million—above the national average in per-capita terms—so the positive deviation is qualitative (institutional visibility, international presence) rather than purely numerical.

records.name: Sachsen
records.summary:
Two documented 2025 features raise Sachsen above the German norm for visitor risk around queer visibility: neo-Nazis mounted a counter-protest intended to disrupt Dresden's pride march on 31 May 2025 (the march proceeded); and the state government, with two neighbouring states, co-sponsored a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act after an abuse-of-self-ID court case ('Fall Liebich'), alleging misuse of the self-ID right — an organised, multi-state push to roll back trans self-determination law.

Germany's national protections and functioning rule of law apply unchanged here; the documented counter-action was policed without event cancellation or reported injuries. Earlier assertions of a wider multi-city attack pattern (Bautzen mob sizes, Döbeln prosecutions) lack support in the retained sources and are removed from the record.

sources.summary: TAG24 (31 May 2025): thousands marched through Dresden for CSD while neo-Nazis mounted a counter-protest aimed at disrupting it; the march went ahead. The 2025 far-right disruption signal behind this record's risk elevation.

Antenne Bayern/dpa: Sachsen, Sachsen-Anhalt and Thuringia jointly launched a Länder initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act (SBGG) after the Fall Liebich abuse case, aiming to block misuse of self-ID. Sachsen co-sponsors the organised multi-state push to roll back trans self-determination law — this record's documented legislative-threat signal.

records.name: Buenos Aires
records.summary:
Buenos Aires Province carries the strongest sub-national negative signal in the country: the provincial human-rights ombudsman's 2016 submission to the UN Human Rights Committee documents acts of violence, persecution and harassment by provincial police — or by third parties under police cover — against trans and travesti people during operations in three cities (La Plata, Mar del Plata and Esteban Echeverría), under 'preventive policing' frameworks. sources.summary: Buenos Aires provincial ombudsman's Gender Violence Office (created by Resolución Nº 100/10) submission to the UN Human Rights Committee (June-July 2016 review): documents violence, persecution and harassment by provincial police — or third parties under police cover — against trans and travesti people in Buenos Aires province, in a dedicated section on violence by judicial, state and police agents. This is the record's core 2016 UN-submission claim. Note: 2016-17 UN-review PDFs no longer describe current law — the 2012 federal Gender Identity Law remains in force, but a Dec-2024 national DNU added consent/medical-judicial requirements for minors' gender-affirming care (under litigation).

UNLP thesis documenting the criminalisation of trans and travesti women in Buenos Aires province through drug-offence prosecutions under microtrafficking enforcement, focused on La Plata's Zona Roja — showing that after the 2012 Gender Identity Law formally decriminalised trans presence, security-led street-offence policing became the operative indirect-criminalisation instrument in the province. Regional academic evidence for the record's escalation claim.

Pensamiento Penal legal analysis: rising criminalisation of trans/travesti women in Buenos Aires province, particularly La Plata's Zona Roja, and it records that in 2005 Buenos Aires province assumed jurisdiction over drug-sale and possession offences — the devolution that enabled provincial street-offence and drug-law prosecution as the indirect-criminalisation instrument. Supplies the dated 2005 mechanism behind the record's escalation claim.

Provincial Ombudsman's September 2024 guide to gender-marker rectification for people born in Buenos Aires province: registry rectification steps, including provisions for people born in the province now living elsewhere. Dated local procedure evidence — provincial implementation of the 2012 federal Gender Identity Law's recognition regime.

records.name: Subcarpathian Voivodeship
records.summary:
For a trans traveler the exposure here is social rather than statutory: the local anti-LGBT declarations were never criminal statutes, and every such document in the country had been repealed or invalidated by 24 April 2025, when the county charter that was the country's final surviving holdout was repealed at an extraordinary session; this state/province's own resolution had been repealed on 20 September 2021.

Practical safety is the operative concern: the repeal was forced from outside (the European Commission threatened to withhold regional development funds) rather than produced by a change in local attitudes, so the de facto social climate that generated the resolutions is assessed to persist. Being visibly trans at a public event in an eastern town whose local authority resisted all external pressure until 2025 carries harassment exposure, and the record shows executive intent to exclude a visible LGBTQ public presence - the capital's mayor banned the 2019 equality march on security grounds, the district court overturned the ban, and the march proceeded.

sources.summary: Notes from Poland (27 Apr 2025): the county of Łańcut in southeast Poland (Podkarpackie) — the last local authority in the country with an anti-LGBT resolution — repealed the measure at an extraordinary councillors' session, closing the resolution era; at the wave's peak about one third of Poland's territory was covered by such documents (per the Atlas of Hate mapping project). Dated end-point for the record's 'last holdout' claim.

The Them (23 Sep 2021, updated 29 Sep): Podkarpackie's voivodeship council repealed its 'LGBT-free' resolution on Monday 20 September 2021, alongside Małopolska and Lubelskie — after the European Commission threatened to withhold regional development funds; Podkarpackie replaced its ordinance with a generic anti-discrimination statement. Confirms the record's 2021 voivodeship repeal under EU funding pressure.
